glance: OpenAI has countersued Apple over trade secrets and pressure on shared hardware suppliers, and Volvo Cars has started training humanoid robots at its Ghent plant. Battery-electric cars took 31% of European registrations in October, leaving most carmakers ahead of their CO2 targets. In bearings, SKF Vertevo passed its record date before Monday's listing, and Schaeffler sold part of its Indian unit.
brief:
Good morning. Here is Vertical News for Saturday the twenty-eighth of November, covering Friday.

OpenAI has countersued Apple in California. It accuses Apple of taking trade secrets and of pressuring suppliers that also work on OpenAI's own devices. Apple's original case against OpenAI goes to trial in July 2027.

Volvo Cars has started training Hexagon's AEON humanoid robots at its plant in Ghent. The robots learn by imitation, begin with one task, placing parts into two fixtures, and could do real production work from mid-2027.

And in Europe, battery-electric cars took thirty-one percent of new registrations in October, according to the ICCT. Most carmakers are now ahead of their CO2 targets, while Volkswagen is still about five grams over.

In other news, Bloomberg found banned Nvidia Blackwell racks at a Shanghai data centre. Adobe says Thanksgiving online sales hit a record 7.1 billion dollars, and shoppers coming from AI tools were seventy-four percent more likely to buy. The UK financial regulator says Meta declined to test its Muse shopping agent in a sandbox.

Stellantis will stop three French plants for weeks over Christmas. The Guangzhou motor show has opened with more than eleven hundred vehicles, almost two thirds of them new-energy models.

In bearings, SKF Vertevo passed its record date and starts trading in Stockholm on Monday, and Schaeffler sold six and a half percent of Schaeffler India for about 314 million euros. Finally, Evident has launched the EPOCH 700 ultrasonic flaw detector, which saves inspections in an open file format.

That's the brief. Have a good weekend.

stories.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple, claiming trade-secret theft and pressure on shared hardware suppliers
stories.why: The fight over AI devices is now about who controls the hardware supply chain, not just the software.
body: OpenAI has filed a countersuit against Apple in a California court, according to the Financial Times. It accuses Apple of taking trade secrets and of threatening suppliers that are also working on OpenAI's own upcoming devices. The filing answers a lawsuit Apple brought in July 2026 against OpenAI, its hardware unit io Products and two former Apple employees.

OpenAI's case says Apple let staff keep company files on personal devices and cloud accounts, and in October OpenAI had already claimed that a former employee who went back to Apple sent more than 100 confidential files about unreleased hardware to personal accounts. Apple has asked for a preliminary injunction, has won wider access to evidence, and says its own investigation found no OpenAI confidential material. Apple's original case is set for trial on 19 July 2027.

For product teams, the dispute shows how quickly AI companies are moving into physical devices, and how contested the small pool of contract manufacturers and component suppliers has become. Expect supplier contracts and staff mobility between hardware teams to be checked much more closely.

stories.headline: Volvo Cars starts training Hexagon's AEON humanoid robots at its Ghent plant
stories.why: A Swedish carmaker is testing humanoids on real assembly tasks, with production use planned from mid-2027.
stories.source: Volvo Cars · The Next Web · Tech Times
body: Volvo Cars has begun training AEON humanoid robots from Hexagon Robotics at its car plant in Ghent, Belgium, the first Volvo factory to try humanoids. Volvo's own engineers teach the robots by imitation learning: the robot watches how a task is done and copies it. The first job is narrow on purpose. The robot places components into two fixtures with high precision, and harder tasks will be added only once each step works reliably.

The AEON is 1.65 metres tall, weighs 60 kg, moves on wheels at up to 2.4 metres per second and can carry 10 kg. A factory pilot is planned for the first half of 2027, when more units arrive, with real production work targeted from mid-2027. Volvo's manufacturing chief Magnus Nilsson says the aim is to take over the most physically demanding work.

For automotive engineers, the useful detail is the method: a single fixture-loading task, a 10 kg payload limit and a staged sign-off before scaling. That is a realistic template for validating humanoids against takt time and quality targets, rather than a broad promise of general-purpose robots.

stories.headline: Battery-electric cars reach 31% of new registrations in Europe in October, and most carmakers are ahead of CO2 targets
stories.why: Compliance pressure on the 2025–2027 CO2 targets is easing for most groups, but not for Volkswagen.
body: New figures from the International Council on Clean Transportation show battery-electric cars took 31% of new registrations in October across the EU, Norway and Iceland. Over the first ten months of 2026 the share rose seven points to 25%. Germany is at 29% year to date, France at 32%, Spain at 12%, Italy at 8% and Poland at 5%. Cars with only a combustion engine fell nine points to 28%.

Since January 2025, manufacturer pools have averaged about 1 g CO2/km below their 2025–2027 target. BYD, Tesla, BMW, Toyota, Stellantis and five others already comply, and Volkswagen, SAIC and Hyundai are on track. Volkswagen, the biggest pool, is still about 5 g/km over. Mercedes-Benz grew its electric share fastest of the seven largest carmakers, up 11 points, but remains among the weakest on CO2.

The ICCT warns that once targets are met, carmakers have little reason to push EV sales further. For suppliers of e-axle, bearing and battery parts, that suggests volumes may follow regulation more than demand until the next target step.

stories.headline: Banned Nvidia Blackwell racks turn up at a Shanghai data centre, Bloomberg reports
stories.why: Export controls on AI chips are leaking, which is likely to bring even tighter rules on cloud and server sales.
stories.source: Bloomberg via The Next Web · Engadget
body: Bloomberg reports that two Chinese companies installed Nvidia's restricted Blackwell hardware at a Shanghai data centre linked to Alice Huang, the founder of Singapore-based Megaspeed. The evidence comes from loan filings to Chinese regulators. One firm, Shanghai Shuoyao, pledged a GB300 NVL72 rack as collateral for a loan of 96 million yuan, about 14 million dollars. A second firm described a GB200 server at the site and listed 32 H200 servers.

Megaspeed is under US investigation over suspected chip smuggling and was added to a US blacklist this week. Bloomberg found no evidence that Megaspeed itself shipped the hardware, and neither Megaspeed nor Nvidia replied. Local media say the site could eventually hold up to 800,000 servers. The report follows Nvidia's halt of server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia earlier in the week.

For European companies buying AI compute, the practical effect is more paperwork: stricter end-user checks, possible permit requirements for large overseas clusters, and slower delivery of high-end servers.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving online sales hit a record 7.1 billion dollars, and shoppers arriving from AI tools convert 74% better
stories.why: AI assistants are becoming a real sales channel, and product pages need to work for them.
stories.source: Adobe Analytics via GSM Global News · TheFly
body: Adobe Analytics says US shoppers spent a record 7.1 billion dollars online on Thanksgiving Day, up 10.4% on last year and above Adobe's own 6.9 billion forecast. Mobile devices accounted for 63.2% of spending. Adobe expects 12.9 billion dollars on Black Friday and a record 15.1 billion on Cyber Monday.

The striking figure is AI traffic. Visits to US retail sites from AI-powered sources such as chat assistants rose 162% year on year. Those visitors were 74% more likely to buy and 72% more likely to add items to their cart than other visitors. Adobe's data covers more than one trillion visits to retail sites.

For product and UX teams, this supports investing in structured product data, clear pricing and fast checkout that work well when an assistant has already done the research. It also means analytics should separate AI-referred visitors, who arrive further along in their decision than typical search traffic.

stories.headline: UK financial watchdog says Meta declined to test its Muse shopping agent in a regulatory sandbox
stories.why: Regulators are starting to treat AI agents that buy things as financial services in their own right.
body: The UK Financial Conduct Authority says Meta turned down its offer to jointly test the Muse personal agent in the FCA's sandbox before the UK launch on 24 November. The FCA's head of innovation, Colin Payne, said the regulator will now watch Muse after launch instead. Muse can search websites, fill in forms and make purchases. Meta says users must approve each purchase and email, and that the agent cannot see passwords or card details.

The FCA said this week that AI agents handling transactions may need authorisation, and it plans a policy sprint on agentic commerce. The Bank of England separately warned that advanced agents could become a risk to financial stability.

For teams designing agent features, approval steps, audit logs and clear liability for wrong purchases are moving from good practice to likely regulatory requirements in the UK, and probably in the EU too.

stories.headline: Stellantis will stop its Sochaux, Rennes and Mulhouse plants for weeks over December and January
stories.why: Weak European demand and Chinese competition are turning into lost production days for French plants and their suppliers.
body: Stellantis is again halting production for several weeks at three French plants, citing a difficult European market and aggressive competition. Mulhouse stops on 4, 7 and 8 December and from 23 December to 11 January. Rennes stops from 18 December to 5 January, possibly longer. Sochaux stops on 3, 4, 7 and 8 December and from 19 December to 11 January 2027.

The same sites already paused for five to 15 days each this autumn, two of them because of EV battery shortages. Sochaux plans to end its night shift in January, affecting about 500 temporary workers, and unions in Rennes fear half a shift could go in 2027. Stellantis registrations in wider Europe fell 8% to 144,786 cars in October, according to ACEA data.

For suppliers in the Peugeot, Citroën and Opel chain, including drivetrain and bearing suppliers, the stoppages mean lower call-offs through the turn of the year and more uncertainty in 2027 planning.

stories.headline: Guangzhou motor show opens with 1,106 vehicles, 64% of them new-energy models
stories.why: China's product cadence keeps setting the pace that European carmakers and suppliers must answer.
body: The 24th Guangzhou International Motor Show opened on 27 November at the Canton Fair Complex and runs until 6 December. More than 1,000 brands fill over 240,000 square metres. Of the 1,106 vehicles on show, 707 are new-energy vehicles, or 63.9%, up from 58% last year, and 115 models are making their first appearance.

Hyundai used the show to unveil a compact electric SUV show car for China, alongside a concept and a facelift. BYD with its Denza, Yangwang and Fang Cheng Bao brands, NIO, XPeng, Li Auto, Leapmotor, Zeekr and Xiaomi all brought new cars. Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Honda and Nissan are also exhibiting.

For European engineers, the share of new-energy launches and the number of premieres are a reminder of how short Chinese development cycles have become. Many of these models, or their platforms, are expected to reach Europe within one or two years.

stories.headline: Schaeffler sells 6.5% of Schaeffler India for about 314 million euros to cut debt
stories.why: The bearing and drivetrain group is turning a strong Indian unit into cash for its balance sheet.
body: Schaeffler placed a 6.5% stake in Schaeffler India with institutional investors on 26 November. It sold about 10.16 million shares at 3,493 rupees each, raising net proceeds of about 314 million euros after taxes and fees. The parent group's holding falls from 74.13% to about 67.63%, and Schaeffler says it will keep at least two-thirds of the Indian company.

The money will go towards reducing net debt and strengthening the equity ratio. Schaeffler India runs five plants and sells FAG and INA bearings and LuK clutch products, competing with SKF, NSK and Timken in a growing market. The sale follows an October notice that Schaeffler was reviewing its holding, and comes weeks after the group announced 3,460 job cuts and five site closures in Europe.
For buyers and engineers, the move underlines India's growing role as a bearing production and engineering base for European groups, while the European footprint shrinks.

stories.headline: SKF Vertevo passes its record date as an SKF executive warns about Chinese bearing makers
stories.why: SKF's automotive bearing business becomes a separate listed company on Monday.
body: Friday 27 November was the record date for SKF's spin-off of its automotive business, SKF Vertevo. Shareholders receive one Vertevo share for every five SKF shares of the same series, and trading on Nasdaq Stockholm starts on 1 December under the tickers SKFVER A and SKFVER B. The Swedish financial supervisor approved the listing prospectus.

The new company starts from a difficult position. In the first nine months of 2026, Vertevo's sales were about 18.0 billion kronor, down from 19.1 billion, with an operating loss of 707 million kronor. It targets an adjusted operating margin above 6% in the medium term and 8% or more in the long term, and does not expect to pay a dividend for 2026. On the same day, Bearing News reported an SKF executive in Sweden warning about Chinese competition, uncertain energy prices and Europe's technology dependence.
For OEM purchasers, Vertevo becomes a separate counterpart for wheel-end, driveline and e-axle bearings, with its own cost pressure and pricing logic.

stories.headline: Evident launches the EPOCH 700 portable ultrasonic flaw detector with open inspection files
stories.why: Open, verifiable data files make ultrasonic results easier to audit and reuse in digital quality systems.
body: Evident Inspection Technologies, the former Olympus NDT business, has launched the EPOCH 700, a new portable ultrasonic flaw detector. It is described as the first in its class to save inspections in the open .nde file format, so data can be checked and reused outside the vendor's own software. The instrument holds EPRI PDI qualification for key nuclear procedures such as weld examination, flaw sizing and bolt inspection.

The hardware uses 24-bit A-scan digitisation, a high-dynamic-range receiver and a new high-resolution display. It combines a touchscreen with a rotary knob and direct-access buttons, so inspectors can work with couplant on their gloves. Evident positions it mainly for weld inspection. No independent comparison with earlier EPOCH models or rival instruments has been published.

For quality teams in bearing and drivetrain production, open file formats matter because they make it easier to feed manual ultrasonic results into traceability systems and AI-based defect analysis alongside in-line inspection data.

watch.title: SKF Vertevo listing
watch.text: SKF's automotive spin-off starts trading on Nasdaq Stockholm on Monday 1 December. The first days of trading will show how investors value a loss-making automotive bearing business.

watch.title: Cyber Monday and AI traffic
watch.text: Adobe forecasts a record 15.1 billion dollars in US online sales on 30 November. Watch whether the AI-referral growth seen on Thanksgiving holds.

watch.title: UK rules for shopping agents
watch.text: The FCA plans a policy sprint on agentic commerce after Meta declined sandbox testing of Muse. Its outcome could set an early template for regulating agents that pay.
